mcqs.q: When counting forwards, which number comes just after 49?

mcqs.q: Counting backwards, which number comes just after 57?
mcqs.why: Counting backwards means one less each time, and 57 - 1 = 56, so 56 comes just after 57.

mcqs.q: Which number comes just after 88 when counting forwards?
mcqs.why: Counting forwards means one more each time, and 88 + 1 = 89, so 89 comes just after 88.

mcqs.q: Which number comes just before 10 when counting forwards?
mcqs.why: The number just before 10 is one less than 10, and 10 - 1 = 9, so it is 9.

mcqs.q: Counting backwards from 99 down to 1, which number is counted last?
mcqs.why: Backward counting from 99 goes down and down and stops at 1, so 1 is the last number counted.

mcqs.q: Counting forwards: 63, 64, ______. Which number comes next?
mcqs.why: Counting forwards adds one each time, and 64 + 1 = 65, so the next number after 64 is 65.

mcqs.q: Counting backwards: 90, 89, ______. Which number comes next?
mcqs.why: Counting backwards takes away one each time, and 89 - 1 = 88, so the next number is 88.

lessons.title: Place Value — Tens and Ones
lessons.notes_html:
Place Value (page 22)

Place value tells us the position / place of a digit in a number. Value of a digit depends on its place in a number. Example: Sara has 9 pencils, she got one more. Now she has 10 pencils. One bundle of 10 pencils means One ten. 10 ones make 1 ten.

Place value example — Sara's pencils: 9 + 1 = ?

Step 1: Sara has 9 pencils.
Step 2: She gets 1 more pencil.
Step 3: 9 + 1 = 10.
Step 4: 10 pencils make one bundle of 10, which is 1 ten.

Answer: 10 pencils = 1 ten

Key points (page 22): 10 ones make 1 ten. 10 is the smallest 2 digit number.

Position of a digit (page 23)

In number 10, the place value of 0 is 0 ones and the place value of 1 is 1 ten. Example — count the beads together: the beads group into 10 and 3. Now these are 1 group of 10 and one group of 3. Total number of beads = 13. The place value of 1 is 1 ten. The place value of 3 is 3 ones. (Note: the book prints '1 ones' here by mistake; the correct value is 3 ones, since there are 3 single beads.) Example — place value of 35: the Tens box holds 3 ten-strips and the Ones box holds 5 single squares. The place value of 3 is tens and 5 is ones: 35 = 3 tens + 5 ones.

Learning Tasks 1 (page 24) — Count tens and ones and write the number

(1) 2 ten-strips and 4 ones

Step 1: Count the ten-strips: there are 2 strips of 10.
Step 2: 2 tens = 20.
Step 3: Count the single squares: there are 4 ones.
Step 4: 20 + 4 = 24.

Answer: 24 — 2 Tens, 4 Ones

(2) 3 ten-strips and 6 ones

Step 1: Count the ten-strips: there are 3 strips of 10.
Step 2: 3 tens = 30.
Step 3: Count the single squares: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 ones.
Step 4: 30 + 6 = 36.

Answer: 36 — 3 Tens, 6 Ones

(3) 4 ten-strips and 6 ones

Step 1: Count the ten-strips: there are 4 strips of 10.
Step 2: 4 tens = 40.
Step 3: Count the single squares: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 ones.
Step 4: 40 + 6 = 46.

Answer: 46 — 4 Tens, 6 Ones

(4) 7 ten-strips and 4 ones

Step 1: Count the ten-strips: there are 7 strips of 10.
Step 2: 7 tens = 70.
Step 3: Count the single squares: there are 4 ones.
Step 4: 70 + 4 = 74.

Answer: 74 — 7 Tens, 4 Ones

Learning Tasks 2 (page 25) — Count the objects and write the number

Count the stars

Step 1: Count the full rows: there are 5 rows of 10 stars.
Step 2: 5 rows of 10 = 50 stars.
Step 3: Count the scattered stars beside the rows: there are 10 stars.
Step 4: 50 + 10 = 60.

Answer: 60 stars

lessons.title: Ordering Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
Ordering Numbers (page 26)

Arranging the numbers from smaller to bigger is increasing order. Example: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Arranging the numbers from bigger to smaller is decreasing order. Example: 46, 45, 44, 43, 42, 41. Key point: Increasing order of numbers is also called ascending order. Decreasing order of numbers is also called descending order.

Learning Task 1 (page 27) — Arrange the numbers in increasing order

(a) 25, 22, 24, 17 in increasing order

17, 22, 24, 25 — start from the smallest (17), then 22, then 24, then the biggest (25).

(b) 50, 40, 70, 60 in increasing order

40, 50, 60, 70 — start from the smallest (40), then 50, then 60, then the biggest (70).

(c) 28, 27, 29, 26 in increasing order

26, 27, 28, 29 — start from the smallest (26), then 27, then 28, then the biggest (29).

Learning Task 2 (page 27) — Arrange the numbers in decreasing order

(a) 72, 73, 74, 71 in decreasing order

74, 73, 72, 71 — start from the biggest (74), then 73, then 72, then the smallest (71).

(b) 75, 80, 70, 65 in decreasing order

80, 75, 70, 65 — start from the biggest (80), then 75, then 70, then the smallest (65).

(c) 91, 92, 89, 90 in decreasing order

92, 91, 90, 89 — start from the biggest (92), then 91, then 90, then the smallest (89).

mcqs.q: Arranging numbers from smaller to bigger is called ______ order.
mcqs.why: When numbers are arranged from smaller to bigger, each next number is bigger, and this is called increasing order.

mcqs.q: Increasing order is also called ______ order.
mcqs.why: The notes say increasing order of numbers is also called ascending order, like going up the stairs.

mcqs.q: 25, 22, 24, 17 in increasing order starts with which number?

mcqs.q: 50, 40, 70, 60 in increasing order ends with which number?
mcqs.why: In increasing order the biggest number comes last; among 50, 40, 70 and 60 the biggest is 70.

mcqs.why: In decreasing order we start from the biggest number; among 72, 73, 74 and 71 the biggest is 74.

mcqs.q: Decreasing order is also called ______ order.

mcqs.q: 28, 27, 29, 26 in increasing order starts with which number?

mcqs.q: 91, 92, 89, 90 in decreasing order ends with which number?
mcqs.why: In decreasing order the smallest number comes last; among 91, 92, 89 and 90 the smallest is 89.

mcqs.q: Arranging numbers from bigger to smaller is called ______ order.
mcqs.why: When numbers are arranged from bigger to smaller, each next number is smaller, and this is called decreasing order.

mcqs.q: In the increasing order 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, the first number 3 is the ______ of them all.
mcqs.why: Increasing order starts from the smallest number, so the first number 3 is the smallest of them all.

More, Less and Equal (page 30)

Bano has 4 candies. Amjad has 6 candies. Amjad has more candies. Bano has less candies. Then Amjad has 4 candies and Bano has 4 candies. So Amjad and Bano have equal candies.

Ordinal number describe the order or position of things. Let's observe the running race and describe their position order like 'first', 'second', 'third' up to tenth. Ordering the numbers in increasing and decreasing order. Identifying the place value of specific digit in 2-digit numbers. Identifying the position of objects using ordinal number (First, Second, Third...). Identify more or less by comparing the number of objects in two groups. Vocabulary used: Numbers, more, less, counting, forward, backward, place value, ones, tens, increasing, decreasing, ordinal number, ascending, descending.

lessons.title: How Many More and How Many Less
lessons.notes_html:
Learning Outcomes

Students' learning outcomes (page 37): After completing this unit, students will be able to: Find recall and use of addition and subtraction facts to 20; Compare numbers to find how many more and how many less; Add and subtract numbers mentally and in written form including: Up to three 1-digit numbers, 2-digit numbers and tens; Add and subtract 2-digit numbers mentally and in written form including: 2 digit numbers and 1-digit numbers (without regrouping), Two 2-digit numbers (without regrouping); Solve real world problem with additions and subtraction using concrete objects and pictorial representations (involving missing numbers, money, quantities and measures).

How Many More (page 38)

Let's compare number of pencils and sharpeners. Numbers of pencils = 5. Number of sharpeners = 3. How many pencils are more than sharpeners? = 2. 5 is more than 3. 5 is 2 more than 3.

Activity (page 38): Let us compare 5 and 8. Count the numbers from 5 to 8. 8 is 3 steps forward from 5. So 8 is 3 more than 5.

Learning Task 1 (page 39) — Compare the following group of objects and tell how many more one is from other

(a) 9 pencils and 6 sharpeners

Step 1: Count the pencils: there are 9.
Step 2: Count the sharpeners: there are 6.
Step 3: 9 - 6 = 3.

Answer: 9 is 3 more than 6 (given as the worked example in the book)

(b) 13 ice creams and 8 ice creams

Step 1: Count the first group: there are 13 ice creams.
Step 2: Count the second group: there are 8 ice creams.
Step 3: 13 - 8 = 5.

Answer: 13 is 5 more than 8

(c) 15 footballs and 7 balloons

Step 1: Count the footballs: there are 15.
Step 2: Count the balloons: there are 7.
Step 3: 15 - 7 = 8.

Answer: 15 is 8 more than 7

(d) 14 books and 11 dolls

Step 1: Count the books: there are 14.
Step 2: Count the dolls: there are 11.
Step 3: 14 - 11 = 3.

Answer: 14 is 3 more than 11

How Many Less (page 40)

Let's compare number of flowers and butterflies. Numbers of flowers = 5. Number of butterflies = 2. How many butterflies are less than flowers? = 3. 2 is less than 5. 2 is 3 less than 5.

Let's compare number of pencils and sharpeners. Numbers of pencils = 5. Number of sharpeners = 4. How many pencils are more than sharpeners? The book's box prints 2 here, but 5 - 4 = 1, so the correct value is 1: 5 is 1 more than 4. 4 is less than 5. 4 is 1 less than 5. (The book's own text below the box confirms 1 — the box value 2 is a book error, flagged here.)

Learning Task 1 (page 41) — Compare the group of objects and tell how many less one is from other

(a) 7 bats and 4 balls

Step 1: Count the bats: there are 7.
Step 2: Count the balls: there are 4.
Step 3: 7 - 4 = 3.

Answer: 4 is 3 less than 7 (the book's printed frame reads '7 is ___ less than 4', which is reversed — the smaller number comes first in a 'less than' sentence)

(b) 5 strawberries and 3 apples

Step 1: Count the strawberries: there are 5.
Step 2: Count the apples: there are 3.
Step 3: 5 - 3 = 2.

Answer: 3 is 2 less than 5 (the book's printed frame reads '5 is ___ less than 3', which is reversed)

(c) 14 books and 11 dolls

Step 1: Count the books: there are 14.
Step 2: Count the dolls: there are 11.
Step 3: 14 - 11 = 3.

Answer: 11 is 3 less than 14

lessons.title: Addition of 1-Digit Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
Addition of 1-Digit Number (page 42)

Addition means to put things together. 5 candies and 4 candies makes 9 candies: 5 + 4 = 9. 3 dates, 5 dates and 4 dates makes 12 dates. We can write it as: 3 + 5 + 4 = 12. Key point: The symbol '+' is used for addition and '=' is used for equality.

Learning Task 1 (page 43) — Count, write numbers and add

Step 2: Count the second group: 3 flowers.
Step 3: 5 + 3 = 8.

Answer: 8 (given as the worked example in the book)

(b) 4 books + 2 books + 3 books

Step 1: Count the groups: 4 books, 2 books and 3 books.
Step 2: 4 + 2 = 6.
Step 3: 6 + 3 = 9.

Answer: 9 books

(c) 4 dolls + 3 dolls

Step 1: Count the first group: 4 dolls.
Step 2: Count the second group: 3 dolls.
Step 3: 4 + 3 = 7.

Answer: 7 dolls

Step 1: Start at 7.
Step 2: Count 2 steps forward: 8, 9.

Answer: 9

(b) 9 + 0

Step 1: Adding zero leaves the number unchanged.
Step 2: 9 + 0 = 9.

Answer: 9

(c) 6 + 3

Step 1: Start at 6.
Step 2: Count 3 steps forward: 7, 8, 9.

Answer: 9

mcqs.why: Add step by step: 3 + 5 = 8 and then 8 + 4 = 12, so the three groups make 12 dates in all.

Addition of 2-Digit Number and Tens (page 44)

Adding 12 and 20

Step 3: Add the ones: 7 ones + 0 ones = 7 ones.
Step 4: 7 tens and 7 ones = 77.

Answer: 77

Step 3: Add the ones: 2 ones + 3 ones = 5 ones.
Step 4: 4 tens and 5 ones = 45.

lessons.title: Subtraction
lessons.notes_html:
Subtraction (page 50)

Subtraction means to take away from the collection. 5 Biscuits, take away 2: Biscuits left = 3 (5 - 2 = 3). 7 Rose flowers, take away 5: Rose flowers left = 2 (7 - 5 = 2). When we take away we subtract.

Subtraction (page 51)

Apples on the tree = 7. Apples fall from the tree = 2. How many apples left = 5. This can be written as: 7 - 2 = 5. Key point: '-' is subtraction symbol. '-' is also called minus. Total candies are 4. Crossed candies are 2. Remaining candies are 2 (4 - 2 = 2).

Subtraction of 1-Digit Numbers (page 52)

Look at these mangoes: Total mangoes are = 7. Take away mangoes = 4. Remaining mangoes = 3. We can write it as: 7 - 4 = 3.

Step 2: Count 5 steps back: 8, 7, 6, 5, 4.

Step 2: Count 3 steps back: 7, 6, 5.

lessons.notes_html:
Mental Subtraction (page 58)

Haris has Rs. 36. He gave Rs. 15 to his sister. How many rupees are left with him? Let's subtract numbers mentally. Step I: Separate tens and ones: 36 is 30 + 6, 15 is 10 + 5. Step II: Subtract tens and ones separately: 30 - 10 = 20, 6 - 5 = 1. Step III: Add the result: 20 + 1 = 21. So Rs. 21/- are left.

Step 2: Step II: Subtract tens and ones separately: 20 - 10 = 10, 9 - 4 = 5.
Step 3: Step III: Add the result: 10 + 5 = 15.

Answer: 15 pencils

Learning Outcomes

Students' learning outcomes (page 84): After completing this unit, students will be able to recognize, name and write fractions: half (1/2), quarter (1/4), two-quarter (2/4) and three-quarter (3/4) of a length, shape, set of objects or quantity using pictorial representations.

Fractions (page 85) — Half

Each part of a whole is called a fraction. A fraction is a part of a whole. A whole can be divided into 2 equal parts or 4 equal parts. One part out of two equal parts of a whole is half. We express one half as 1/2 and read it as 'one over two' or 'one by two'.

One Quarter (page 86)

One part out of four equal parts of a whole is one quarter. We express one quarter as 1/4 and read it as 'one over four' or 'one by four'.

Learning Outcomes

Students' learning outcomes (page 104): After completing this unit, students will be able to measure and compare the length of only two objects using non-standard units; use mathematical language to compare the mass of two or more objects; measure and compare the mass of objects using non-standard units; measure and compare the capacity of objects using non-standard units; read and write temperature to the nearest appropriate unit in degrees centigrade (C) using pictorial representation and relating the temperature scale to the number line.

Length (page 105) — Long, Longer, Longest

Length tells us how long something is from one end to the other. Long: car. Longer: bus. Longest: truck. Long: short pencil. Longer: middle pencil. Longest: longest pencil.

b) Carrots: which is long, which is longest?

Colour the rightmost carrot Red (long) and the middle carrot Green (longest). The small left carrot is neither.

c) Ropes: which is long, which is longest?

Colour the middle rope Red (long) and the rightmost rope Green (longest). The small left rope is neither.

Height (page 107) — Short, Shorter, Shortest

Height is the measurement of something or someone from top to bottom. Short pencil: the tallest of the three pencils shown. Shorter pencil: the middle pencil. Shortest pencil: the smallest pencil.

Tall: the smallest candle. Taller: the middle candle. Tallest: the largest candle.

An analogue clock has two hands. The hour hand is shorter than the minute hand. In the example the hour hand is at 3 and the minute hand is at 12, so the time is 3 o'clock. Learning Outcomes

Identification of Pictograph (page 149)

lessons.title: Probability — Likelihood
lessons.notes_html:
Probability / Likelihood (page 152)

Probability means how likely something is to happen. When you toss a coin there are two possible results: heads and tails. A mug has 5 pens: 4 blue pens and 1 red pen. Picking the blue pen is more likely (4 out of 5 pens are blue). Picking the red pen is less likely (only 1 out of 5 pens is red). Picking a yellow pen is impossible (there is no yellow pen in the mug).

Learning Task (page 153) — Likelihood of the balls in the box

The box has 10 balls in total: 4 green balls and 6 blue balls.

More likely: which colour?

Blue ball (6 out of 10 balls are blue) — the book already fills this row.

Less likely: which colour?

Green ball (only 4 out of 10 balls are green).

Impossible: which colour?

Any colour not in the box, for example a red ball (there are no red balls in the box).

lessons.title: Glossary — Key Words
lessons.notes_html:
Ascending Order: numbers from smallest to largest. Addition: the process of calculating 2 or more numbers. Bar Graph: a graph which displays units of data with blocks. Backward: the process of counting downward. Currency: the system of money in general use. Coin: metal money is a coin. Cone: a 3-D figure. Circle: a 2-D figure, a round plain figure. Cube: a 3-D symmetrical shape. Descending Order: numbers from largest to smallest. Division: the process of being separated equally. Difference: the result of subtracting one number from another. Fraction: parts of a whole. Forward Counting: counting sequentially from a lower number to a higher number. Half: one of the two equal parts of a whole. Multiplication: the process of calculating the product of two or more numbers. Ordinal Number: a number defining the position of something. Ordering: placing objects into a particular arrangement. Quarter: each of 4 equal parts of a whole. Subtraction: the process of taking one number away from the other. Sum: the result after adding two or more numbers. Square: a 4-sided shape in which all sides are equal. Triangle: a plain figure with 3 sides and 3 corners.

(2) Page 81, Review 1(c): both '5 times 3' and '3 times 5' equal 15; the book's grouping (3 groups of 5) is 3 times 5. (3) Page 92, Review 1(iv): the circle shows 3/4 coloured but none of the printed options is three-quarters — answered as three-quarters with no option ticked. (4) Thermometer readings (pages 114, 116) are approximate readings from the printed scales, stated as 'about'. (5) Page 127, Review 2, second clock (12:25) and page 128, first clock (1:30) are the unit's only clocks that are not on the hour. (6) Page 147, sphere/cylinder/cone vertices-faces-edges are given at Grade 1 level (sphere: 0 vertices, 1 curved surface, 0 edges; cylinder: 0 vertices, 3 faces, 2 edges; cone: 1 vertex, 2 faces, 1 edge).
